title: Sort Even and Odd Indices Independently
description:
You are given an integer array `nums`. Positions are numbered from 0. Sort the values that sit at the even positions (0, 2, 4, ...) in increasing order, and separately sort the values at the odd positions (1, 3, 5, ...) in decreasing order. Every value stays in its own group (even or odd position), so the even positions only ever swap with other even positions. Return the new array.

Example: for [4, 1, 2, 3], the even positions hold 4 and 2, which become 2 and 4. The odd positions hold 1 and 3, which become 3 and 1. The result is [2, 3, 4, 1].
hints: Use two separate lists: one for the even-position values and one for the odd-position values. Sort each, then write them back into the same positions.

test_cases.explanation: Even positions 4,2 sort to 2,4; odd positions 1,3 sort (descending) to 3,1.
Each group has one value, so nothing changes.

title: Replace Elements with Greatest Element on Right Side
description:
Given an integer array `arr`, replace every element with the greatest value found strictly to its right. The last element has nothing to its right, so it becomes -1. Return the updated array.

Example: for [17, 18, 5, 4, 6, 1], the first element becomes 18 (the largest value after it), the second becomes 6, and so on. The last element becomes -1.
hints: Walk from the right end to the left, keeping track of the largest value seen so far.

test_cases.explanation: 18 is the largest value to the right of 17; 6 is the largest to the right of 4; the last element gets -1.
A single element has nothing to its right, so the result is -1.

title: Count Pairs Whose Sum Is Less Than Target
description:
Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, count how many pairs of indices (i, j) exist with i < j and nums[i] + nums[j] < target. Each pair is counted once, and the same index is never used twice in one pair.

Example: for nums = [-1, 1, 2, 3, 1] and target = 2, the qualifying pairs are (-1, 1), (-1, 2) and (-1, 1). That gives 3.
hints: Sorting the array lets you use two pointers from both ends: if the two ends sum to less than the target, every element between them also works with the left end.

test_cases.explanation: The pairs (-1,1), (-1,2) and (-1,1) each sum to less than 2.
Pairs such as (-6, 2) with sum -4 and (-7, 3) with sum -4 both fall below -2.

title: Number of Lines To Write String
description: You are writing a string `s` on a sheet of paper that can hold at most 100 pixels per line. `widths[k]` is the width in pixels of the letter with index k in the alphabet (widths[0] is 'a', widths[1] is 'b', and so on). Write the letters from left to right. When the next letter would make the current line wider than 100 pixels, start a new line instead. Return `[lines, lastLineWidth]`: the total number of lines used and the width in pixels of the last line.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
hints: Keep a running width for the current line. Before adding a letter, check whether it would exceed 100; if so, count a new line and reset the width.

test_cases.explanation: Each letter is 10 pixels. Ten letters fill one line of 100 pixels, so 26 letters need 3 lines; the last line holds 6 letters, which is 60 pixels.
The total width is 30 + 30 + 30 + 8 = 98 pixels, which still fits on one line.

title: Check if All Characters Have Equal Number of Occurrences
description:
Given a string `s`, count how many times each character appears. Return true if every character that appears in the string appears the same number of times, and false otherwise.

Example: in "abacbc", 'a', 'b' and 'c' each appear twice, so the answer is true. In "aaabb", 'a' appears three times but 'b' appears only twice, so the answer is false.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
hints: Count each character, then check whether all the counts are the same (a set of the counts should have exactly one element).

test_cases.explanation: a, b and c each appear exactly twice.
Only one character exists, so every character trivially has the same count.
The letters x, y and z each appear exactly twice.
a appears 3 times but b appears 2 times.

title: Greatest Common Divisor of Strings
description:
A string `t` divides a string `s` if `s` can be built by repeating `t` some number of times (for example, "ABC" divides "ABCABC"). Given two strings `str1` and `str2`, return the longest string that divides both of them. If no such string exists, return an empty string.

Example: "ABC" divides both "ABCABC" and "ABC", so for str1 = "ABCABC" and str2 = "ABC" the answer is "ABC". For str1 = "LEET" and str2 = "CODE", no string divides both, so the answer is "".
constraints: str1 and str2 consist of uppercase English letters.
hints: If the two strings can be divided by a common string, then str1 + str2 must equal str2 + str1. In that case the answer's length is the gcd of the two lengths.

test_cases.explanation: "ABC" repeated twice gives "ABCABC" and once gives "ABC".
"AB" repeated gives both strings, and it is the longest such string.
The two strings share no repeating pattern.

title: Largest Odd Number in String
description:
You are given a string `num` made of digits. Return the largest substring of `num` (a contiguous piece that starts at the beginning of the string or after some digits) that represents an odd number. A number is odd when its last digit is odd. Return an empty string if no odd substring exists.

Example: in "52", the substring "5" is odd and it is the largest odd piece, so the answer is "5". In "4206", every substring ends in an even digit, so the answer is "".
constraints: num contains only digits and does not have leading zeros.
hints: A longer prefix is always bigger, so look for the rightmost odd digit. Cutting the string right after that digit gives the largest odd number.

test_cases.explanation: Cutting after the 5 gives "5", which is odd. "52" itself ends in 2 and is even.
The whole string ends in 7, which is odd, so the whole string is the largest odd piece.
Every digit is even, so no prefix is odd.

title: Remove Vowels from a String
description:
Given a string `s`, delete every vowel (the letters 'a', 'e', 'i', 'o' and 'u') and return the result. Keep every other character in its original order.

Example: "hello" becomes "hll".
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only.
hints: Build a new string by including only the characters that are not in the set of vowels.

test_cases.explanation: The vowels e and o are removed, leaving h, l, l.
Every vowel (a, e, i, o, u) is removed and the other letters keep their order.
Every character is a vowel, so the result is empty.

title: Count Words Containing a Letter
description:
You are given an array of strings `words` and a single lowercase letter `letter`. Count how many of the words contain that letter at least once.

Example: with words = ["leet", "code"] and letter = "e", both words contain an 'e', so the answer is 2.
constraints: letter is a single lowercase English letter.
hints: For each word, check whether the letter is part of it.

test_cases.explanation: Both words contain an 'e'.
Only "abc" and "aaaa" contain an 'a'.

title: Maximum Count of Positive and Negative Integers
description:
Given an array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, count the positive numbers and the negative numbers separately. Zero counts as neither. Return the larger of the two counts.

Example: for [-2, -1, -1, 1, 2, 3], there are 3 negatives and 3 positives, so the answer is 3. For [-3, -2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2], there are 3 negatives and 2 positives, so the answer is 3.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: Count each sign directly in one pass, or use binary search since the array is sorted.

test_cases.explanation: There are 3 negatives and 3 positives, so the larger count is 3.
There are 3 negatives and 2 positives; zeros do not count.

title: Sum of Digits in Base K
description:
Given a positive integer `n` written in base 10, convert it to base `k`, then add up its digits in base k. Return that sum. Base k means each digit is between 0 and k - 1.

Example: 34 written in base 6 is 54 (5 times 6 plus 4). The digits add up to 9, so the answer is 9.
hints: Repeatedly take n modulo k (that is the lowest base-k digit), add it to the total, then divide n by k.

test_cases.explanation: 34 in base 6 is 54, and 5 + 4 = 9.
10 in base 10 is 10, and 1 + 0 = 1.

title: Check if Number Is a Sum of Powers of Three
description:
Given an integer `n`, decide whether it can be written as a sum of distinct powers of three, such as 3^0 = 1, 3^1 = 3, 3^2 = 9, and so on. Each power may be used at most once. Return true if it is possible, and false otherwise.

Example: 12 = 9 + 3, which uses 3^2 and 3^1, so the answer is true. 21 cannot be written this way, so the answer is false.
hints: Write n in base 3. The number works exactly when no digit is 2.

test_cases.explanation: 12 = 9 + 3, both distinct powers of three.
21 would need the digit 2 in base 3, so it cannot be formed.
2 needs two copies of 1, and each power can be used only once.

title: Build Array from Permutation
description:
You are given a zero-based permutation `nums` (every value from 0 to n - 1 appears exactly once). Build a new array `ans` of the same length where ans[i] = nums[nums[i]] for every index i. Return `ans`.

Example: for nums = [0, 2, 1, 5, 3, 4], ans[0] = nums[nums[0]] = nums[0] = 0, and ans[1] = nums[nums[1]] = nums[2] = 1.
constraints: nums is a permutation of 0 to nums.length - 1.
hints: Read the value at position nums[i] for each i. You can do this with a single pass and no extra data structure.

test_cases.explanation: ans[1] = nums[2] = 1, ans[2] = nums[1] = 2, and so on.
ans[0] = nums[5] = 4, ans[1] = nums[0] = 5, and so on.

title: Sort the People
description:
You are given an array `names` and an array `heights` of the same length, where names[i] is the name of a person whose height is heights[i]. All heights are distinct. Return the names ordered from the tallest person to the shortest.

Example: names = ["Mary", "John", "Emma"] and heights = [180, 165, 170] give ["Mary", "Emma", "John"], because 180 > 170 > 165.
hints: Pair each name with its height, sort the pairs by height from largest to smallest, then keep only the names.

test_cases.explanation: Tallest is Mary (180), then Emma (170), then John (165).
Bob is 185 and Alice is 155, so the taller Bob comes first.

title: Minimum Bit Flips to Convert Number
description:
A bit flip changes a single bit of a number from 0 to 1 or from 1 to 0. Given two integers `start` and `goal`, return the minimum number of bit flips needed to turn `start` into `goal`.

Example: 10 is 1010 in binary and 7 is 0111. They differ in three bit positions, so the answer is 3.
hints: XOR-ing the two numbers gives a 1 in every position where they differ. Count those 1 bits.

test_cases.explanation: 10 = 1010 and 7 = 0111; they differ in 3 positions.
3 = 011 and 4 = 100; all three bits differ.

title: Largest Local Values in a Matrix
description:
You are given an n x n integer matrix `grid`. Build an (n - 2) x (n - 2) matrix `maxLocal` where maxLocal[i][j] is the largest value inside the 3 x 3 block of `grid` whose top-left corner is at row i, column j. Return `maxLocal`.

Example: the top-left 3 x 3 block of the example grid contains the values 9, 9, 8, 5, 6, 2, 8, 2, 6, so maxLocal[0][0] = 9.
hints: Use two nested loops for the top-left corners, and inside each, take the maximum of the nine cells in the 3 x 3 block.

test_cases.explanation: The 3x3 blocks have maxima 9, 9 (top row) and 8, 6 (bottom row).
The center value 2 is inside every block that touches it.

title: Minimum Moves to Convert String
description:
You are given a string `s` made of 'X' and 'O' characters. In one move you may pick any three consecutive characters and turn all of them into 'O'. Return the minimum number of moves needed so that the string contains no 'X' characters at all.

Example: for "XXOX", one move on the first three characters turns them into "OOOX", and a second move on the last three covers the final 'X'. The answer is 2.
hints: Scan from left to right. When you hit an 'X', one move is needed, and that move also covers the next two characters, so you can skip ahead by three.

test_cases.explanation: One move covers all three characters.
The first move covers positions 0-2, and the second covers the last X.

title: Delete Characters to Make Fancy String
description:
A fancy string is one where no three consecutive characters are equal. You may delete characters from the string `s`. Delete as few characters as needed to make it fancy, keeping the remaining characters in order. Return the resulting string. The answer is unique.

Example: "aaabaaaa" becomes "aabaa", because each run of 'a' is cut down to at most two.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Keep a result list. Before adding a character, check whether the last two characters you kept are both equal to it; if so, skip it.

test_cases.explanation: The three e's are reduced to two, giving "leetcode".
Each run of a's is cut down to two.

title: Minimum Amount of Time to Fill Cups
description:
There is a water dispenser with three cups of different sizes, and `amount[i]` is the number of cups of water cup i needs. In one second you can fill up to two different cups at the same time (each by one cup of water). Return the minimum number of seconds needed to fill all cups.

Example: amount = [1, 4, 2]. The total is 7 cups, so at least 4 seconds are needed (two at a time). The biggest single cup needs 4 seconds too, so the answer is 4.
hints: Two numbers of the same kind can be handled per second, so the answer is at least half the total (rounded up), and at least the largest single amount.

test_cases.explanation: Half of the total 7 rounds up to 4, which equals the largest amount.
Total 13 gives 7 seconds, which is more than the largest amount 5.
Only one cup needs water, and it takes one cup per second.

title: Buy Two Chocolates
description:
A shop sells chocolates at the prices in the array `prices`. You have `money` dollars and want to buy exactly two chocolates, spending as little as possible. If you can afford two chocolates, return the money you have left after buying the cheapest pair. If you cannot afford any pair, return the original amount of money, since you must not be in debt.

Example: prices = [1, 2, 2] and money = 3. The cheapest pair costs 1 + 2 = 3, leaving 0.
hints: The cheapest two chocolates are the two smallest prices. Check whether their total fits in the money.

test_cases.explanation: The cheapest pair costs exactly 3, leaving 0.
The cheapest pair costs 5, which is more than 3, so the money is kept.

title: Kth Distinct String in an Array
description:
A distinct string is one that appears exactly once in the array `arr`. Read the array from left to right and return the k-th distinct string. If there are fewer than k distinct strings, return an empty string.

Example: in ["d", "b", "c", "b", "c", "a"], the distinct strings in order are "d", "a". With k = 2, the answer is "a".
constraints: arr[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Count how often each string appears, then go through the array in order and keep only the strings with count 1.

test_cases.explanation: Distinct strings in order are d, a; the second one is a.
All three are distinct, so the first is aaa.
Only b is distinct, so there is no third one.

title: Decode the Message
description:
A secret substitution alphabet is built from a 26-letter `key` string (ignore spaces; the first time a letter appears in the key it is assigned to 'a', the next new letter to 'b', and so on). Each letter in `message` is replaced using that mapping. Spaces stay as spaces. Return the decoded message.

Example: with the key "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog", the first letter 't' maps to 'a', 'h' maps to 'b', and 'e' maps to 'c'.
constraints: key contains lowercase English letters and spaces.
key contains every English letter at least once.
hints: Build a dictionary from each key letter (in first-appearance order) to the next letter of the alphabet, then translate each message character with it.

inputs.key: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog

test_cases.explanation: The mapping t->a, h->b, e->c, q->d and so on decodes the message to "this is a secret".
Each letter's position in the key gives the plain letter: r is the 11th key letter, which stands for k, and so on.
With the plain alphabet as key, each letter maps to itself.

title: Reverse Prefix of Word
description:
Given a string `word` and a character `ch`, find the first occurrence of `ch` in `word`. If it exists, reverse the part of `word` from the start up to and including that position, and keep the rest unchanged. If `ch` does not appear, return `word` unchanged.

Example: word = "abcdefd" and ch = 'd'. The first 'd' is at index 3, so "abcd" is reversed to "dcba", giving "dcbaefd".
constraints: word consists of lowercase English letters.
ch is a lowercase English letter.
hints: Find the index of the first occurrence, then build the answer from the reversed prefix followed by the untouched remainder.

test_cases.explanation: The prefix abcd is reversed to dcba.
The prefix xyxz (up to the first z) is reversed to zxyx, and the rest xe stays the same.
The letter z does not appear, so the word is unchanged.

title: Make the String Great
description:
A string is called good if it contains no two adjacent characters that are the same letter in different cases (for example, "aA" or "Bb"). Whenever you find such a pair, delete both characters, and repeat until the string is good. Return the final good string. The result is unique.

Example: "leEeetcode" becomes "leetcode" after removing the "Ee" pairs one at a time. "abBAcC" collapses completely to an empty string.
constraints: s contains only lowercase and uppercase English letters.
hints: Use a stack. Compare each new character with the top of the stack; if they are the same letter with different case, pop instead of pushing.

test_cases.explanation: Removing the adjacent pair e and E leaves "leetcode".
Each adjacent pair cancels, leaving nothing.
Pp is removed entirely, so the empty string is returned.

title: Count Substrings with Only One Distinct Letter
description:
Given a string `s`, count the substrings that contain only one distinct letter. A substring is any contiguous piece of `s`. Each occurrence counts separately, even if two substrings have the same text.

Example: in "aaaba", the substrings with a single distinct letter are "a" (4 times), "aa" (2 times), "aaa" (once) and "b" (once). That is 8 substrings in total.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Split the string into runs of the same letter. A run of length L contributes L * (L + 1) / 2 substrings.

test_cases.explanation: The run aaa contributes 6 substrings, plus 1 for the b and 1 for the final a.
A single run of length 10 gives 10 * 11 / 2 = 55.

title: Shifting Letters
description:
You are given a lowercase string `s` and an integer array `shifts` of the same length. For each index i, shifts[i] means: shift the letter at positions 0 through i forward in the alphabet by shifts[i]. A shift wraps around, so 'z' shifted by 1 becomes 'a'. All of these shifts are applied to the original string, and they add up: a letter at position p is shifted by the sum of shifts[i] for every i >= p. Return the final string.

Example: s = "abc", shifts = [3, 5, 9]. Position 2 ('c') is shifted by 9. Position 1 ('b') is shifted by 5 + 9 = 14. Position 0 ('a') is shifted by 3 + 5 + 9 = 17. The result is "rpl".
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Go from the right end to the left, keeping a running total of shifts (taken modulo 26). Each letter is shifted by the running total at its position.

test_cases.explanation: The total shifts are 17, 14 and 9 for positions 0, 1 and 2, giving r, p and l.
The total shifts for positions 0, 1 and 2 are 6, 5 and 3, giving g, f and d.
No shifts are applied, so the string is unchanged.

title: Lexicographically Smallest Palindrome
description:
You are given a lowercase string `s`. In one operation you may change any single character to another letter. Make `s` a palindrome (it reads the same forward and backward) using the fewest changes, and among all palindromes that need the fewest changes, choose the lexicographically smallest one. Return that palindrome.

Example: "egcfe" has mismatched pairs (e, e are fine; g and f differ at positions 1 and 3; the middle letter c is fine). Changing each mismatched pair to the smaller letter gives "efcfe".
constraints: s consists of only lowercase English letters.
hints: Compare the characters at mirrored positions. Each mismatched pair needs exactly one change, and the best choice is to change both to the smaller of the two letters.

test_cases.explanation: The pairs (e,e), (g,f) and the middle c: g and f become f, giving efcfe.
The pairs (a,d) and (b,c) both become the smaller letter, giving abba.
The string is already a palindrome, so no change is needed.

title: Minimum Length of String After Operations
description:
You are given a string `s`. In one operation you may choose an index i such that the character s[i] appears somewhere to the left of i and somewhere to the right of i. Delete the closest occurrence of s[i] to the left of i and the closest occurrence of s[i] to the right of i. The character at index i itself is not deleted. Repeat as many times as you like, and return the minimum possible length of the string.

Example: "abaacbcbb" can be reduced to length 5. Each letter with an odd count can be cut down to a single copy, and each letter with an even count can be cut down to two copies.
constraints: s consists only of lowercase English letters.
hints: Each letter is independent. Keep removing groups of three until fewer than three copies remain: that leaves 1 copy if the count is odd and 2 copies if it is even.

test_cases.explanation: a: 3 copies -> 1; b: 4 copies -> 2; c: 2 copies -> 2; total 5.
Only two copies exist, so nothing can be removed.
Each letter has only one copy, so the length stays 3.

title: Divide Array Into Equal Pairs
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` with an even length. Split the array into pairs such that every pair contains two equal values, and every element is used in exactly one pair. Return true if this is possible, and false otherwise.

Example: [3, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2] can be split into (3, 3), (2, 2) and (2, 2), so the answer is true.
hints: Every value must occur an even number of times for the pairs to work out.

test_cases.explanation: The value 3 appears twice and the value 2 appears four times, so both pair up.
The value 1 appears twice, which makes one pair.
Every value appears an even number of times: 5 six times, 1 twice, 2 twice and 3 six times.
Every value appears once, so no pair of equal values exists.

title: Smallest Number With All Set Bits
description:
A number has all set bits if its binary form is made only of 1s, such as 1 ("1"), 3 ("11"), 7 ("111") and 15 ("1111"). Given an integer `n`, return the smallest number that is at least `n` and has all set bits.

Example: for n = 5, the candidates in order are 1, 3, 7, ... The first one that is at least 5 is 7.
hints: Keep building the value 1, 3, 7, 15, ... (each step is multiplying by 2 and adding 1) until it reaches n.

test_cases.explanation: The sequence is 1, 3, 7; 7 is the first value at least 5.
15 is the first all-ones number that is at least 10.
7 itself already has all set bits.

title: Count Integers With Even Digit Sum
description:
Given a positive integer `num`, count how many integers x from 1 to num (inclusive) have an even digit sum. The digit sum of a number is the sum of its decimal digits.

Example: for num = 4, the numbers are 1 (sum 1), 2 (sum 2), 3 (sum 3), 4 (sum 4). Only 2 and 4 have an even digit sum, so the answer is 2.
hints: Compute the digit sum of each number from 1 to num and count the even ones. The input is small, so checking every number is fast enough.

test_cases.explanation: Only 2 and 4 have an even digit sum.
The 14 numbers from 1 to 30 with an even digit sum are 2, 4, 6, 8, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19, 20, 22, 24, 26 and 28.
1 has digit sum 1, which is odd, so the count is 0.

title: Number of Ways to Split Array
description:
You are given an integer array `nums`. A valid split is an index i (0 <= i < n - 1) such that the sum of the elements from index 0 to i is greater than or equal to the sum of the elements from i + 1 to the end. Count the valid splits.

Example: for [10, 4, -8, 7], the split after index 0 gives left sum 10 and right sum -5 (valid). The split after index 1 gives left sum 14 and right sum -1 (valid). The split after index 2 gives left sum 6 and right sum 7 (not valid). So the answer is 2.
hints: Keep a running prefix sum. The suffix sum is the total minus the prefix sum, so you can check each split in constant time.

test_cases.explanation: Splits after index 0 and 1 are valid; the split after index 2 is not.
Splits after index 1 and 2 are valid.
Left sum is -5 then -10, both less than the right side, so no split works.

title: Prime Pairs with Target Sum
description:
Given an integer `n`, find all pairs of prime numbers [x, y] such that x + y = n and x <= y. Return the pairs sorted by x in increasing order. If there are no such pairs, return an empty list.

Example: for n = 10, the pairs are [3, 7] and [5, 5], because 3 + 7 = 10 and 5 + 5 = 10. The answer is [[3, 7], [5, 5]].
hints: Try each x from 2 to n/2. Its partner is y = n - x. Check whether both are prime using trial division up to the square root.

test_cases.explanation: 3 + 7 and 5 + 5 are the only pairs of primes that add up to 10.
4 = 2 + 2 is the only split, and both are prime.
The only pair of primes that adds up to 7 is 2 + 5.

title: Chalkboard XOR Game
description:
Alice and Bob play a game with the numbers in `nums` written on a chalkboard. They take turns, and Alice goes first. On a turn, a player erases exactly one number. If erasing a number makes the XOR of all the remaining numbers equal to 0, that player loses. If a player starts their turn when the XOR of all the numbers is already 0, that player wins immediately. Return true if Alice wins when both players play optimally.

Example: nums = [1, 1, 2]. Erasing a 2 would leave [1, 1] with XOR 0, so Alice avoids that and erases a 1. The game continues, and with best play Bob wins, so the answer is false.
hints: If the XOR of all numbers is already 0, Alice wins. If the count of numbers is even, Alice wins as well. Otherwise, the answer is false.

test_cases.explanation: The XOR of 0,1,2,3 is 0 right away, so Alice wins.
The XOR is already 0 (1 xor 2 xor 3), so Alice wins immediately.
The XOR is 2, not 0, and the count is odd, so Alice cannot win and the result is false.
One number has a non-zero XOR and an odd count, so Alice must erase it and Bob wins.

title: Concatenation of Consecutive Binary Numbers
description:
Given an integer `n`, write the binary representations of the numbers 1, 2, ..., n one after another, in that order, to form one long binary string. Interpret that string as a binary number and return its value modulo 10^9 + 7.

Example: for n = 3, the string is "1" + "10" + "11" = "11011", which equals 27.
hints: Keep a running value. Appending number i means shifting the value left by the bit length of i, then adding i. Take the result modulo 10^9 + 7 at each step.

test_cases.explanation: The string is just "1", which equals 1.
The string "11011" equals 27.
Writing 1 to 12 in binary and joining them gives one very long binary number; its value modulo 1000000007 is 505379714.

title: Count Distinct Integers After Reverse Operations
description:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers. For each number, append its reversed digits to the array (for example, 13 adds 31, and 10 adds 1 because leading zeros disappear). Count how many distinct integers are in the array after all the reversed numbers are added. Duplicates count only once.

Example: nums = [1, 13, 10, 12, 31]. Reversals give 1, 31, 1, 21, 13. The distinct values are 1, 13, 10, 12, 31, 21, so the answer is 6.
hints: Use a set. For each number, add both the number and its reversed digits. Reversing with strings and converting back to an integer removes leading zeros automatically.

test_cases.explanation: The set becomes {1, 13, 10, 12, 31, 21}, which has 6 elements.
Reversing 100 gives 1 (leading zeros are dropped) and reversing 200 gives 2, so the set is {100, 200, 1, 2}.
Every copy is 2, and its reverse is also 2, so only one distinct value exists.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Binary Array Elements Equal to One I
description:
You are given a binary array `nums` (values are 0 or 1). In one operation you may choose any three consecutive elements and flip each of them (0 becomes 1, and 1 becomes 0). Return the minimum number of operations needed to make every element equal to 1, or -1 if it is impossible.

Example: nums = [0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0]. Flip positions 0-2 to get [1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0]. Flip positions 1-3 to get [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0]. Flip positions 3-5 to get [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. That took 3 operations, so the answer is 3.
hints: Scan from left to right. Whenever you see a 0 at position i (and i is not among the last two), flipping the window starting at i is forced, so do it. At the end, check whether the last two values are 1.

test_cases.explanation: Flipping windows starting at indices 0, 1 and 3 makes everything 1.
Flipping from the left gives [1, 1, 1, 0, 0], and the last two zeros cannot be covered by a window of three, so the answer is -1.
After the forced flips the final element stays 0, and no window can start there to flip it, so the answer is -1.

title: Number of Subarrays With GCD Equal to K
description:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, count the contiguous subarrays whose greatest common divisor (GCD) is exactly k. The GCD of a subarray is the largest positive integer that divides every element in it.

Example: in [9, 3, 1, 2, 6, 3] with k = 3, the subarrays with GCD 3 are [9, 3], [3] (at index 1), [6, 3], and [3] (the last element). That is 4 subarrays in total.
hints: For each starting index, extend the subarray one element at a time and update the running GCD. Once the GCD drops below k, it can never return to k, so you can stop.

test_cases.explanation: The four subarrays with GCD 3 are [9,3], [3], [6,3] and [3].
Every subarray has GCD 6: three single elements, two pairs and the full array, which makes 6.
The only subarray is [4], whose GCD is 4, not 2.

title: Maximum Subarray Sum With Length Divisible by K
description:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray whose length is a multiple of k (lengths k, 2k, 3k, ...). If no subarray has such a length, return 0.

Example: nums = [1, 2] and k = 1. Every length is a multiple of 1, so the best choice is the whole array, with sum 3. For nums = [1, -2, 3] and k = 2, the valid lengths are 2, so the subarrays [1, -2] (sum -1) and [-2, 3] (sum 1) are considered, and the answer is 1.
hints: Use prefix sums. A subarray from index i to j has sum prefix[j+1] - prefix[i], and its length is (j+1) - i. Only pairs where the length is a multiple of k are allowed.

test_cases.explanation: The whole array has length 2, a multiple of 1, and sums to 3.
Subarrays of length 2 have sums -1 and 1, so the best is 1.
No subarray has a length that is a multiple of 4, so the answer is 0.

title: Longest Alternating Subarray
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `threshold`. Find the longest contiguous subarray that satisfies all of these rules: it starts with an even number; every element is less than or equal to `threshold`; and the parity (even or odd) changes at every step. Return the length of the longest such subarray, or 0 if none exists.

Example: nums = [3, 2, 5, 4] and threshold = 5. The subarray [2, 5, 4] starts with 2 (even), all values are at most 5, and the parity alternates (even, odd, even). Its length is 3.
hints: Start a candidate only at an even value that is at most the threshold. From there, keep extending while each next value is within the threshold and has the opposite parity.

test_cases.explanation: The subarray [2, 5, 4] has length 3 and follows all the rules.
The only even start is 2, and the subarray [2] has length 1.
The subarray [2, 3, 4] has length 3, and 5 is above the threshold.

title: Smallest Value of the Rearranged Number
description:
You are given an integer `num`. Rearrange its digits in any order you like. The result must not start with a zero (unless the result is 0 itself). Return the smallest value that can be obtained. If `num` is negative, the minus sign stays in front, and you should return the smallest value overall, which means the digits of the absolute value should be arranged as large as possible.

Example: for 310, arrange the digits as 103 (not 013, since that starts with zero). For -7605, arrange the digits as 7650 and return -7650.
hints: For a positive number, put the smallest non-zero digit first, then the rest in ascending order. For a negative number, put the digits of its absolute value in descending order.

test_cases.explanation: The smallest non-zero digit 1 goes first, followed by 0 and 3, giving 103.
The digits sorted descending are 7650, so the answer is -7650.
Zero stays zero.

title: Partition Array Such That Maximum Difference Is K
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Split the array into subsequences (the order inside a group does not matter, and every number belongs to exactly one group). In each group, the largest value minus the smallest value must be at most k. Return the minimum number of groups needed.

Example: nums = [3, 6, 1, 2, 5] with k = 2. One group can hold [1, 2, 3], since 3 - 1 = 2, and another holds [5, 6], since 6 - 5 = 1. That is 2 groups, which is the minimum.
hints: Sort the array. Start a group at the smallest unassigned value, and keep adding values while they stay within k of that starting value. Then start a new group.

test_cases.explanation: Groups [1,2,3] and [5,6] work, and one group is not enough.
Group [1,2] and then [3].
The two 2s share one group, while 4 and 5 each need their own, for 3 groups.

title: Divide Array in Sets of K Consecutive Numbers
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Decide whether you can divide the numbers into groups of exactly k numbers, where each group contains consecutive integers (for example, 3, 4, 5, 6 when k = 4). Every number must be used exactly once. Return true if this is possible, and false otherwise.

Example: [1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6] with k = 4 can be split into [1, 2, 3, 4] and [3, 4, 5, 6], so the answer is true.
hints: Always start a group with the smallest remaining number. That number must be the first member of a run of k consecutive values, so remove one of each of the next k values (fail if any is missing).

test_cases.explanation: The groups [1,2,3,4] and [3,4,5,6] use every number once.
The groups [1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 5] and [9, 10, 11] use every number exactly once.
Groups [1,2] and [4,5] each hold consecutive integers, so the answer is true.
4 numbers cannot be split into groups of 3.

title: Minimum Number of Operations to Make Array Empty
description:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers. In one operation you may remove either two elements that have the same value, or three elements that have the same value. Return the minimum number of operations needed to empty the array, or -1 if it is impossible.

Example: [2, 3, 3, 2, 2, 4, 2, 3, 4]. The value 2 appears 4 times (two removals of 2), the value 3 appears 3 times (one removal of 3), and the value 4 appears twice (one removal of 2). That is 4 operations in total.
hints: Handle each value separately. A value with count c needs ceil(c / 3) operations, as long as c is at least 2. A count of 1 can never be removed.

test_cases.explanation: Counts are 4, 3, 2: that needs 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 operations.
A pair of equal values takes one operation.
Five equal values can be removed as a group of three and a group of two, so 2 operations are needed.
The value 1 appears only once, so the array can never be emptied.

title: Maximum Number of Coins You Can Get
description:
There are piles of coins. Repeat the following until no piles remain: pick any three piles, let Alice take the pile with the most coins, you take the pile with the second most coins, and Bob takes the pile with the fewest. Return the maximum number of coins you can collect, given the array `piles` of coin counts.

Example: piles = [2, 4, 1, 2, 7, 8]. Good triples are (2, 7, 8), giving you 7, and (1, 2, 4), giving you 2. Your total is 9.
hints: Sort the piles. Always let Alice take the largest and Bob the smallest, and you take the second largest. The best strategy is to skip the smallest piles and take the second largest of each group of three from the top.

test_cases.explanation: Your picks are 7 and 2, totaling 9.
The only group is 2, 4, 5, so you take 4.
Each round Alice takes the largest pile, you take the next largest and Bob takes the smallest; your piles are 8, 6 and 4, totalling 18.

title: Remove Stones to Minimize the Total
description:
You are given an array `piles` of stone counts and an integer `k`. You must perform exactly k operations. In each operation, choose the pile with the most stones and remove half of its stones, rounding down (so you take floor(x / 2) away, and the pile keeps ceil(x / 2)). Return the smallest possible total number of stones left after the k operations.

Example: piles = [5, 4, 9] and k = 2. First, 9 becomes 5, so piles become [5, 4, 5]. Then one of the 5s becomes 3. The total is 5 + 4 + 3 = 12.
hints: Use a max-heap. Each time, pop the largest pile, reduce it to ceil(x / 2), and push it back.

test_cases.explanation: After two operations the piles are [5, 4, 3], which sums to 12.
Three operations on the largest piles: 7 becomes 4, 6 becomes 3 and then a 4 becomes 2, leaving 2, 3, 3 and 4 with a total of 12.
A pile of 1 becomes 1 after each operation (ceil(1/2) = 1).

title: Ways to Make a Fair Array
description:
You are given an integer array `nums`. Remove exactly one element. After removal, the remaining elements are renumbered from 0. The array is fair if the sum of the elements at even indices equals the sum of the elements at odd indices. Count how many indices, when removed, leave a fair array.

Example: nums = [2, 1, 6, 4]. Removing index 1 gives [2, 6, 4], where the even-index sum is 2 + 4 = 6 and the odd-index sum is 6. That is fair. No other removal is fair, so the answer is 1.
hints: Removing an element shifts the parity of everything after it. Keep prefix sums for even and odd positions, and for the suffix use the parity-swapped values, so each index is checked in constant time.

test_cases.explanation: Only removing index 1 leaves equal even and odd sums.
Removing any of the three gives sums that are equal, so the answer is 3.
No removal creates a fair array.

title: Maximum Length of Subarray With Positive Product
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, find the longest contiguous subarray whose product is positive. The product of an empty or zero-containing subarray is not positive, so such subarrays don't count. Return the length of the longest subarray with a positive product (0 if none exists).

Example: [1, -2, -3, 4] has the whole array as a positive-product subarray, with product 24, so the answer is 4. In [0, 1, -2, -3, -4], the subarray [1, -2, -3] has product 6, so the answer is 3.
hints: Track the longest subarray ending here with a positive product and with a negative product. A positive number extends both; a negative number swaps them; zero resets both.

test_cases.explanation: The whole array has two negatives, so its product is positive.
The subarray [1, -2, -3] has length 3 with a positive product.
The longest positive-product run is [-1, -2], with length 2.

title: Largest Divisible Subset Size
description:
Given a set of distinct positive integers `nums`, find the size of the largest subset in which every pair of numbers satisfies a divisibility rule: for any two numbers a and b in the subset, either a divides b or b divides a.

Example: for [1, 2, 4, 8], the whole set works, because each number divides the next. The answer is 4. For [1, 2, 3], the best subset is [1, 2] or [1, 3], so the answer is 2.
hints: Sort the numbers. Then dp[i] = longest valid chain ending at nums[i]: take the best dp[j] over earlier numbers that divide nums[i], and add 1.

test_cases.explanation: Every number divides the next, so all four fit.
1 with 2, or 1 with 3, gives 2 numbers; 2 and 3 cannot be together.
The numbers 4, 12 and 24 form a chain in which each one divides the next.
No number divides another, so the best is a single number.

title: Count Ways to Build Good Strings
description:
Start with an empty string. You may repeatedly append either `zero` copies of '0' or `one` copies of '1'. A string is good if its length is between `low` and `high` (inclusive). Count the distinct good strings that can be built this way, and return the count modulo 10^9 + 7.

Example: low = 3, high = 3, zero = 1, one = 1. Every string of length 3 made of 0s and 1s can be built, giving 8 good strings.
hints: Let dp[len] be the number of ways to build a string of exactly len characters. dp[len] = dp[len - zero] + dp[len - one], and the answer adds dp[len] for every len in [low, high].

test_cases.explanation: Every binary string of length 3 is buildable: 2^3 = 8.
The good strings are 00 and 11 (length 2) and 000, 011 and 110 (length 3), which makes 5.
Length 6 strings are built from the blocks 000 and 111, giving 000000, 000111, 111000 and 111111.
Neither 2 nor 3 divides length 1, so no string of length 1 can be built.

title: Minimum Score Triangulation of Polygon
description:
You are given the values of the vertices of a convex polygon in clockwise order, as the array `values`. You must cut the polygon into triangles by drawing diagonals between vertices. Each triangle gives a score equal to the product of its three vertex values. The total score is the sum over all triangles. Return the minimum possible total score.

Example: values = [1, 2, 3]. It is already a single triangle, with score 1 * 2 * 3 = 6.
hints: Look at the edge between the first and last vertex. It belongs to exactly one triangle with some middle vertex k. Split the polygon into two smaller polygons and solve each with the same idea.

test_cases.explanation: Only one triangle exists: 1 * 2 * 3 = 6.
Two triangles: diagonal from 3 to 4 gives 3*7*4 + 3*4*5 = 144.
The lowest possible total over all triangulations of this hexagon is 13.

title: Find the Champion I
description:
There are n teams numbered 0 to n - 1. You are given an n x n matrix `grid`. If grid[i][j] == 1, team i is stronger than team j. Otherwise grid[i][j] == 0. A champion is a team that is stronger than every other team. Return the champion's number. The input is guaranteed to contain exactly one champion.

Example: in [[0, 1], [0, 0]], team 0 is stronger than team 1, so the champion is 0.
constraints: For i != j, exactly one of grid[i][j] and grid[j][i] is 1.
hints: For each team, check whether its row is all 1s except on the diagonal. The first such team is the champion.

test_cases.explanation: Team 0 beats team 1, so team 0 is the champion.
Team 1 beats both team 0 and team 2.

title: Find the Champion II
description:
There are n teams numbered 0 to n - 1. You are given a list `edges` where [a, b] means team a is stronger than team b. The relationship is transitive and consistent (there are no cycles). A champion is a team that no other team is stronger than. If exactly one team is a champion, return its number. Otherwise return -1, because the champion cannot be determined.

Example: with n = 3 and edges [[0, 1], [1, 2]], team 0 is never beaten, so it is the champion. With n = 4 and edges [[0, 2], [1, 3], [1, 2]], both team 0 and team 1 are never beaten, so the answer is -1.
constraints: The graph is a directed acyclic graph.
hints: A team is beaten if some edge points to it. Count incoming edges for each team; teams with zero incoming edges are the candidates.

test_cases.explanation: Team 0 is not beaten by anyone, so it is the only champion.
A single team is trivially the champion.
Team 0 beats both other teams and is never beaten, so it is the champion.
Teams 0 and 1 are both never beaten, so the champion is not unique.

title: Closest Node to Given Two Nodes
description:
You are given a directed graph with n nodes where each node has at most one outgoing edge. edges[i] is the node that node i points to, or -1 if node i has no outgoing edge. Given two nodes node1 and node2, find a node x that both can reach, which minimizes the larger of the two distances (the distance from node1 to x and the distance from node2 to x). If several nodes tie, return the one with the smallest index. Return -1 if no node can be reached from both.

Example: edges = [2, 2, 3, -1], node1 = 0, node2 = 1. Node 2 is reached from node 0 in 1 step and from node 1 in 1 step. Its larger distance is 1, which is the best, so the answer is 2.
hints: Follow the single outgoing edges from each start node and record the step count at which each node is first reached. Then compare the two distance lists node by node.

test_cases.explanation: Node 2 is one step from both starting points, which is the best possible.
Node 2 is reached from 0 in two steps and from 2 in zero steps; no better meeting point exists.
Node 2 is 2 steps from node 0 and node 0 is 2 steps from node 2, so both give a worst case of 2; the tie goes to the smaller index, 0.
Nodes 0 and 2 lead to different dead ends, so they never meet.

title: Longest Cycle in Graph
description:
You are given a directed graph with n nodes where each node has at most one outgoing edge. edges[i] is the node that node i points to, or -1 if it has no outgoing edge. A cycle is a path that returns to its starting node. Return the length of the longest cycle in the graph, counted as the number of nodes in it. If there is no cycle, return -1.

Example: edges = [3, 3, 4, 2, 3]. Starting at node 2 you go 2 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2, a cycle of length 3. That is the longest cycle, so the answer is 3.
hints: Walk from each unvisited node while recording the order you visited nodes in this walk. If you reach a node already in the current walk, the cycle length is the difference in their positions.

test_cases.explanation: The cycle 2 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 has 3 nodes.
The cycle between 0 and 1 has length 2.
There are two separate cycles, 0 to 1 to 2 to 0 and 3 to 4 to 5 to 3, and each has 3 nodes.
The path 0 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1 ends at node 1, which has no outgoing edge, so there is no cycle.

title: Count Nodes With the Highest Score
description:
A tree has n nodes numbered 0 to n - 1, given by the array `parents`, where parents[i] is the parent of node i. The root is node 0, and parents[0] is -1. If you remove a node, the tree splits into several parts: the subtree of each child, plus the rest of the tree (if any). The score of a node is the product of the sizes of these parts. Return how many nodes have the highest score.

Example: parents = [-1, 2, 0, 2, 0]. Removing node 1 leaves one part of size 4 (the other nodes), so its score is 4. Nodes 3 and 4 also score 4, while node 2 scores 2 and node 0 scores 3. Three nodes tie for the highest score, so the answer is 3.
hints: Compute each subtree's size with one traversal. The parts after removing node i are its child subtrees and the remaining n - size[i] nodes (skip that part if it is empty).

test_cases.explanation: Three nodes tie for the highest score.
Nodes 0 and 1 both have score 2, the highest.

title: Count Ways to Place Houses
description:
A street has n plots on each side, so there are 2n plots in total: n on the left and n on the right. On each side, you may leave a plot empty or build a house on it. Houses on the same side may not be next to each other (two adjacent plots on one side cannot both have houses). The two sides are independent. Return the number of ways to place the houses, modulo 10^9 + 7. Note that an empty street (no houses at all) counts as a valid placement.

Example: for n = 1, each side has 2 choices (empty or a house), so the total is 2 * 2 = 4.
hints: First count the valid arrangements for one side: that count follows the Fibonacci numbers. Then square it, since the two sides are independent.

test_cases.explanation: Each side has 2 options, so 2 * 2 = 4.
One side has 3 valid patterns (00, 10, 01), so 3 * 3 = 9.
Each side has 5 valid patterns of length 3 with no two adjacent houses, so 5 * 5 = 25.

title: Longest Common Subsequence of Three Strings
description:
Given three strings s1, s2 and s3, find the length of the longest string that is a subsequence of all three. A subsequence keeps the original order of characters but does not need to be contiguous.

Example: for "abc", "abc" and "abc", the whole string is common, so the answer is 3. For "abc", "def" and "ghi", there is no shared letter, so the answer is 0.
constraints: Strings contain only lowercase English letters.
hints: Extend the usual two-string LCS table into three dimensions. When the three current characters match, add 1 to the diagonal value; otherwise take the best of the three ways to skip one character.

test_cases.explanation: All three strings are identical, so the answer is 3.
The only letter shared by all three strings is a.
The subsequence hl appears in all three strings.
No letter is shared by all three strings.

title: Number of Ways to Wear Different Hats
description:
There are n people and 40 hats, numbered 1 to 40. `hats[i]` is the list of hats that person i likes. You must give each person exactly one hat that they like, and no two people may wear the same hat. Return the number of ways to do this, modulo 10^9 + 7.

Example: hats = [[3, 4], [4, 5], [5]]. Person 2 only likes hat 5, so person 2 must take 5. That leaves hat 4 for person 1 (who likes 4 and 5), and then person 0 must take 3. Only this one assignment works, so the answer is 1.
constraints: All values in hats[i] are distinct.
hints: Process hats one at a time. Keep a DP over which set of people already has a hat, using a bitmask. For each hat, either leave it unused or give it to a person who likes it and does not yet have a hat.

test_cases.explanation: Only one full assignment exists: 3, 4, 5.
Person 0 can take 1, 3 or 5, and person 1 takes 3 or 5, giving 4 valid combinations.
Each of the 4 people can wear any of the 4 hats, so the assignments number 4! = 24.
Both people only like hat 1, so they cannot both wear it.

title: Minimum Operations to Make the Array Alternating
description:
An array is alternating if the values at all even indices are equal, the values at all odd indices are equal, and the even-index value differs from the odd-index value. In one operation you may change any element to any value. Return the minimum number of operations needed to make `nums` alternating.

Example: [3, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3] has even positions holding 3, 3, 4 and odd positions holding 1, 2, 3. Changing the 2 to 1, the 4 to 3, and the last 3 to 1 gives [3, 1, 3, 1, 3, 1], which is alternating. That takes 3 changes, so the answer is 3.
hints: Count how often each value appears at even positions and at odd positions. Try the most common even value with the most common odd value (or the next most common) when they are different.

test_cases.explanation: Keeping 3 at even positions and 1 at odd positions needs 3 changes.
Keep 2 at odd positions and use 1 at even positions; change the other 2 values.
Keep the 1s at the even positions and change the two 1s at the odd positions to 2, which is 2 changes.
Already alternating, since the two positions hold different values.

title: Check If Word Is Valid After Substitutions
description:
A string is valid if it can be built from an empty string by repeatedly inserting the substring "abc" anywhere in it. Given a string `s`, return true if it is valid, and false otherwise.

Example: "aabcbc" is valid. Start from "", insert "abc" to get "abc", then insert "abc" between the letters 'a' and 'bc' to get "aabcbc". "abcabcababcc" is also valid. "abccba" is not valid.
hints: Use a stack. Push each letter. Whenever the top three letters are a, b, c in that order, remove them. The string is valid if the stack ends empty.

test_cases.explanation: Built by inserting abc inside an existing abc.
Each abc can be removed in turn until nothing is left.
After removing abc from the front, cba cannot be reduced.

title: Smallest String With a Given Numeric Value
description:
The numeric value of a letter is its position in the alphabet: a = 1, b = 2, ..., z = 26. The numeric value of a string is the sum of the values of its letters. Given two integers n and k, return the lexicographically smallest string of length n whose numeric value is exactly k.

Example: for n = 3 and k = 27, the string "aay" has value 1 + 1 + 25 = 27, and no smaller string of length 3 reaches 27.
hints: Start with n copies of 'a'. Then add the remaining value from the end of the string toward the front, giving each position at most 25 extra (up to 'z').

test_cases.explanation: "aay" has value 27 and is the smallest such string.
Fill from the end with the largest letters allowed: z and z, then s (19) to use the rest, leaving the front as a and a.

title: Count Number of Maximum Bitwise-OR Subsets
description:
The bitwise OR of a list of numbers is the OR of all of them together. Given an integer array `nums`, find the largest possible bitwise OR over all non-empty subsets of `nums`. Return how many non-empty subsets achieve that maximum OR. Subsets are chosen by position, so two subsets with equal values but different positions count separately.

Example: nums = [3, 1]. The maximum OR is 3, achieved by the subset [3] and the subset [3, 1]. The answer is 2.
hints: Since the array is small, you can try every subset with a bitmask. Compute the OR of each subset and count those matching the maximum.

test_cases.explanation: Subsets [3] and [3, 1] both have OR 3.
Every non-empty subset has OR 2, so all 7 non-empty subsets count.
The maximum OR is 7. Any subset that contains 5 and at least one of 3 or 2 reaches 7, which gives 6 subsets.

title: Maximum Number of Operations With the Same Score I
description:
You are given an integer array `nums`. In each operation, you delete the first two elements and record their sum as the operation's score. You may keep operating as long as at least two elements remain, but every operation must have the same score as the first one. Return the maximum number of operations you can perform.

Example: nums = [3, 2, 1, 4, 5]. The first two elements sum to 5, and the next two (1 + 4) also sum to 5. The last element is left alone, so the answer is 2.
hints: Remove the first two elements repeatedly. Stop as soon as a pair's sum differs from the first pair's sum.

test_cases.explanation: Both pairs (3,2) and (1,4) sum to 5.
The second pair sums to 7, not 5, so only one operation is allowed.
There is one pair, (1, 1), with sum 2, so one operation is possible.

title: Apply Operations to an Array
description:
You are given an array `nums`. Go through the array from left to right. For each index i (from 0 to n - 2), if nums[i] equals nums[i + 1], double nums[i] and set nums[i + 1] to 0. After all of these steps, move every 0 to the end of the array while keeping the other values in their original order. Return the final array.

Example: [1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 0]. At index 1 the two 2s merge: [1, 4, 0, 1, 1, 0]. At index 3 the two 1s merge: [1, 4, 0, 2, 0, 0]. Moving the zeros to the end gives [1, 4, 2, 0, 0, 0].
hints: Do the pairwise pass first, in order, then collect the nonzero values and add zeros at the end.

test_cases.explanation: At index 1 the two 2s merge into 4 and a 0. At index 3 the two 1s merge into 2 and a 0.
No neighbouring pair is equal, so only the reordering of zeros applies.

title: Separate the Digits in an Array
description:
Given an array of positive integers `nums`, return an array of their digits in the same order as the numbers appear, with each number's digits kept in order. Digits are kept separate, so 13 contributes the digits 1 and 3.

Example: [13, 25, 83, 77] becomes [1, 3, 2, 5, 8, 3, 7, 7].
hints: Convert each number to a string and read off its characters as integers.

test_cases.explanation: Each number's digits are listed in order.
Every number here is a single digit, so the list is unchanged.

title: Count of Interesting Subarrays
description:
You are given an integer array `nums`, an integer `modulo`, and an integer `k`. A subarray is interesting if the number of indices i in the subarray with nums[i] % modulo == k, call it cnt, satisfies cnt % modulo == k. Count the interesting subarrays and return the total.

Example: nums = [3, 2, 4], modulo = 2, k = 1. Elements that satisfy nums[i] % 2 == 1 are only the 3. The subarrays [3], [3, 2] and [3, 2, 4] each contain cnt = 1, and 1 % 2 == 1, so all three are interesting. The answer is 3.
hints: Keep a running count of matching elements taken modulo `modulo`. A subarray is counted when the difference between two prefix values equals k (mod modulo). Store how often each prefix value has appeared.

test_cases.explanation: The subarrays [3], [3,2] and [3,2,4] each contain exactly one odd number.
Only [1] (no multiples of 3, so cnt = 0) and the whole array (cnt = 3) qualify, so the answer is 2.

title: Minimum Cost to Make All Characters Equal
description:
You are given a binary string `s` of length n, made of '0' and '1'. You may flip characters in two ways: choose an index i and flip every character from index 0 to i (cost i + 1), or choose an index i and flip every character from index i to n - 1 (cost n - i). Return the minimum total cost to make all characters equal.

Example: "0011". Flipping the prefix ending at index 1 costs 2 and gives "1111". Flipping the suffix starting at index 2 also costs 2 and gives "0000". The answer is 2.
hints: Each place where two neighbouring characters differ must be fixed by one flip, and the cheaper of the two options for that boundary is the prefix or suffix ending/starting at it.

test_cases.explanation: The only boundary is between index 1 and index 2; the cheapest way to fix it costs 2.
Every adjacent pair differs, so several boundaries must be paid for.

title: Minimum Operations to Make Median of Array Equal to K
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. In one operation you may increase or decrease any element by 1. The median of an array is its middle element after sorting; for an even length, it is the larger of the two middle values. Return the minimum number of operations needed so that the median of `nums` equals k.

Example: nums = [2, 5, 6, 8, 5] and k = 4. Sorted, the array is [2, 5, 5, 6, 8] with median 5. Decreasing the two 5s to 4 costs 2 operations. The median becomes 4, so the answer is 2.
hints: Sort the array. The median position is fixed, so you only need to move the middle value to k and fix the elements on the one side that would break the order.

test_cases.explanation: Two elements (the 5s) must come down to 4 to make the median 4.
The median 5 must rise to 7 (cost 2), and the 6 next to it must also rise to 7 to keep the order (cost 1).

title: Maximum Value of an Ordered Triplet I
description:
You are given an integer array `nums`. The value of an ordered triplet of indices (i, j, k) with i < j < k is (nums[i] - nums[j]) * nums[k]. Return the maximum value over all such triplets. If every triplet has a negative value, return 0.

Example: nums = [12, 6, 1, 2, 7]. The triplet (0, 2, 4) gives (12 - 1) * 7 = 77, which is the largest value, so the answer is 77.
hints: The array is small, so you can check every triplet with three nested loops.

test_cases.explanation: (12 - 1) * 7 = 77 is the best triplet.
(10 - 3) * 19 = 133 is the best triplet.
Every triplet here gives a negative or zero value, so the answer is 0.

title: Count Subarrays of Length Three With a Condition
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, count the subarrays of length 3 where the sum of the first and third elements is exactly half of the middle element. In other words, for a subarray [a, b, c], count it when a + c == b / 2.

Example: nums = [1, 2, 1, 4, 1]. The subarray [1, 4, 1] has 1 + 1 = 2, which is half of 4, so it counts. The other subarrays do not satisfy the condition, so the answer is 1.
hints: Check each window of three consecutive values. To avoid fractions, compare 2 * (first + third) with the middle value.

test_cases.explanation: Only [1, 4, 1] satisfies 1 + 1 = 4 / 2.
1 + 1 = 2 is not equal to 1 / 2.

title: Find the Largest Area of Square Inside Two Rectangles
description:
There are n axis-aligned rectangles. Rectangle i has bottom-left corner bottomLeft[i] = [x, y] and top-right corner topRight[i] = [x, y]. For any pair of rectangles, the area where they overlap is also a rectangle. Find the largest square that fits completely inside the overlap of at least two rectangles, and return its area. If no two rectangles overlap, return 0.

Example: take rectangles [1, 1]-[3, 3] and [2, 2]-[4, 4]. Their overlap is [2, 2]-[3, 3], a 1 x 1 area, so the largest square has area 1.
constraints: All coordinates are integers between 1 and 10^7.
hints: For each pair of rectangles, the overlap is between the larger of the left edges and the smaller of the right edges (and similarly for top and bottom). The largest square inside it has side equal to the smaller of its width and height.

test_cases.explanation: The overlap is a 1 x 1 square.
The largest overlap square has area 1.

title: Check If Array Is Good
description:
An array is good for a number n if it has length n + 1, contains each of the values 1 to n - 1 exactly once, and contains the value n exactly twice. Given an array `nums`, return true if it is good for some n, and false otherwise.

Example: [1, 3, 3, 2] is good for n = 3: it has length 4, contains 1 and 2 once, and 3 twice. [2, 1, 3] is not good.
hints: Find the largest value n in the array. Sort the array, and check whether it equals 1, 2, ..., n - 1, followed by n, n.

test_cases.explanation: The sorted array is [1, 2, 3, 3], which is good for n = 3.
n = 1 with the value 1 appearing twice.
With n = 2 the array must hold 1 once and 2 twice, but it holds 3, so it is not good.

title: Minimum Operations to Exceed Threshold Value I
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. In one operation, remove the smallest element of the array. Return the minimum number of operations needed so that every remaining element is at least k.

Example: nums = [2, 11, 10, 1, 3] and k = 10. The elements smaller than 10 are 2, 1 and 3, so three removals are needed. The answer is 3.
hints: Each removal takes out the current smallest element, so you must remove exactly the elements that are smaller than k.

test_cases.explanation: The values 2, 1 and 3 are below 10, so three removals are needed.
No element is below 1, so nothing needs to be removed.

title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. Find the maximum sum of a subarray of length exactly k whose elements are all distinct. Return that maximum sum, or 0 if no such subarray exists.

Example: nums = [1, 5, 4, 2, 9, 9, 9] and k = 3. The subarray [5, 4, 2] has distinct values and sum 11. The subarray [4, 2, 9] has distinct values and sum 15, which is the maximum, so the answer is 15.
hints: Slide a window of size k across the array. Track how often each value appears in the window; a window is valid only when it has k distinct values.

test_cases.explanation: The window [4, 2, 9] has distinct values and sum 15.
Every window of length 3 has repeated values, so the answer is 0.

title: Count Hills and Valleys in an Array
description:
An index i is a hill if its value is strictly greater than the nearest different value on its left and on its right. It is a valley if its value is strictly smaller than the nearest different values on both sides. Equal neighbours belong to the same hill or valley, so count each one only once. Return the number of hills and valleys.

Example: [2, 4, 1, 1, 6, 5]. The 4 is a hill (2 < 4 > 1), the 1 is a valley (4 > 1 < 6), and the 6 is a hill (1 < 6 > 5). The answer is 3.
hints: First remove consecutive duplicate values, then check each remaining middle value against its two neighbours.

test_cases.explanation: Hills at 4 and 6, a valley at 1.
The array is strictly decreasing after removing duplicates, so there are none.

title: Number of Smooth Descent Periods of a Stock
description:
You are given an integer array `prices` where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. A smooth descent period is a contiguous range of days where the price drops by exactly 1 from each day to the next. A single day also counts as a smooth descent period. Return the number of smooth descent periods.

Example: prices = [3, 2, 1, 4]. The periods are [3], [2], [1], [4], [3, 2], [2, 1], [3, 2, 1]. That is 7 periods.
hints: Track how long the current descending run is. Each day adds one new period for each start point in the run, so add the current run length to the total each day.

test_cases.explanation: The run 3, 2, 1 gives 6 periods and [4] adds one more.
No step drops by exactly 1 (8 to 6 is a drop of 2, and 6 to 7 is a rise), so each day is its own period.

title: Minimum Consecutive Cards to Pick Up
description:
You are given an integer array `cards` where cards[i] is the value of the i-th card. A pair of matching cards is two cards with the same value. You must pick up a consecutive block of cards that contains at least one matching pair. Return the minimum number of consecutive cards you need to pick up, or -1 if there is no matching pair.

Example: cards = [3, 4, 2, 3, 4, 7]. The shortest block with a matching pair is [3, 4, 2, 3], which has 4 cards. The answer is 4.
hints: For each card, remember where it last appeared. The block between two equal cards, inclusive, is a candidate, so track the smallest such distance.

test_cases.explanation: The block [3, 4, 2, 3] is the shortest with a repeated card.
All values are different, so no pair exists.

title: Maximum Candies Allocated to K Children
description:
You have `candies` piles of candy, where candies[i] is the number of candies in pile i. You want to share them with k children. Each child must receive the same number of candies, and each child gets candies from one pile only (a pile can be split into several parts, each given to a different child). Return the largest number of candies each child can receive. If it is impossible to give every child at least one candy, return 0.

Example: candies = [5, 8, 6] and k = 3. Each child can get 5 candies: pile 5 gives 1 child, pile 8 gives 1 child with 3 left over, and pile 6 gives 1 child. The answer is 5.
hints: Binary search on the answer x: x is achievable if the sum of candies[i] // x over all piles is at least k.

test_cases.explanation: The answer 5 works, and 6 would leave only 2 children served.
There are only 7 candies for 11 children, so the answer is 0.

title: Maximum Value at a Given Index in a Bounded Array
description:
You want to build an array `nums` of length n with these rules: every value is at least 1; the total of all values is at most maxSum; and neighbouring values differ by at most 1. Among all such arrays, choose one where nums[index] is as large as possible. Return that largest value of nums[index].

Example: n = 4, index = 2, maxSum = 6. The array [1, 2, 2, 1] has sum 6, and nums[2] = 2. A value of 3 at index 2 would need a total above 6, so the answer is 2.
hints: Binary search on the value at the index. For a given peak value, the best array decreases by 1 on each side until it reaches 1, and you can add up both sides in closed form.

test_cases.explanation: The array [1, 2, 2, 1] sums to 6 with value 2 at index 2.
The array [2, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1] sums to 10 with the peak 3 at index 1.

title: Minimum Time to Complete Trips
description:
You are given an array `time` where time[i] is the time in minutes that bus i takes to complete one trip. Each bus works independently and makes trips back to back. Given the total number of trips `totalTrips` that must be completed, return the minimum time needed for the buses together to finish them.

Example: time = [1, 2, 3] and totalTrips = 5. In 3 minutes the buses finish 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 trips, so the answer is 3.
hints: Binary search on the total time t. A given t works if the sum of t // time[i] over all buses is at least totalTrips.

test_cases.explanation: In 3 minutes the buses complete 3 + 1 + 1 = 5 trips.
One bus that takes 2 minutes per trip needs 2 minutes for its first trip.

title: Minimum Number of Days to Eat N Oranges
description:
You have n oranges. Each day you may do exactly one of these: eat one orange; if n is divisible by 2, eat n / 2 oranges; if n is divisible by 3, eat 2 * n / 3 oranges. Return the minimum number of days needed to eat all the oranges.

Example: n = 10. Eat one orange (9 left), then eat 6 of them (3 left), then eat 2 (1 left), then eat the last one. That takes 4 days, so the answer is 4.
hints: From a count x, the best next move is either to remove x % 2 oranges and halve, or to remove x % 3 oranges and divide by three. Use memoization on the recursion.

test_cases.explanation: The path 10 -> 9 -> 3 -> 1 -> 0 takes 4 days.
Eat 3 oranges at once from 6, leaving 3, then 2 at once, then 1: 3 days.

title: Find the Prefix Common Array of Two Permutations
description:
You are given two permutations `a` and `b` of the numbers 1 to n. The prefix common array C has length n, where C[i] is the number of values that appear in both a[0..i] and b[0..i] (counting prefixes of both arrays up to index i). Return C.

Example: a = [1, 3, 2, 4] and b = [3, 1, 2, 4]. At i = 0, the prefixes are [1] and [3]: no common value, so C[0] = 0. At i = 1, the prefixes are [1, 3] and [3, 1]: both values are shared, so C[1] = 2. The full answer is [0, 2, 3, 4].
constraints: a and b are permutations of 1 to n.
hints: Keep two sets of values seen so far. Each time a new value enters a set, check whether it is already in the other set.

test_cases.explanation: The shared count grows as the prefixes expand: 0, 2, 3, 4.
The prefixes {2} and {3} share nothing; at index 1 the value 3 becomes shared, and at index 2 all three values are.

title: Maximum Matrix Sum
description:
You are given an n x n integer matrix. In one operation, you may choose two neighbouring cells (sharing a side) and multiply both values by -1. Repeat as many times as you like. Return the largest possible sum of all values in the matrix after these operations.

Example: [[1, -1], [-1, 1]]. Flip the signs of the two -1s pairwise to make every value positive: the sum is 4.
hints: Each operation changes the sign of two neighbours, so the parity of the number of negatives can only change when a zero is involved. Without zeros, if the count of negatives is odd, one value must stay negative; choose the smallest absolute value for that.

test_cases.explanation: Two negatives can be flipped in pairs, so all values become positive: the sum is 4.
There are three negatives (odd), so the smallest absolute value 1 must stay negative; 18 - 2 = 16.

title: Most Frequent Even Element
description:
Given an integer array `nums`, find the even value that appears most often. If several even values share the highest frequency, return the smallest of them. If there are no even values, return -1.

Example: [0, 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 1]. The even values are 0, 2, 2, 4, 4. Both 2 and 4 appear twice, so the smaller one, 2, is returned.
hints: Count only the even values, then pick the highest count, breaking ties by the smaller value.

test_cases.explanation: 2 and 4 tie at two occurrences; the smaller one, 2, wins.
4 appears three times, the most of any even value.
There are no even values, so the answer is -1.

title: Sum of Squares of Special Elements
description:
You are given a 1-indexed array `nums` of length n. An element nums[i] is special if i divides n (that is, n % i == 0). Return the sum of the squares of all special elements.

Example: nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]. The length is n = 4. The indices that divide 4 are 1, 2 and 4, so the special elements are 1, 2 and 4. Their squares sum to 1 + 4 + 16 = 21.
hints: Loop over the indices 1 to n and keep the ones where n is divisible by the index.

test_cases.explanation: The special indices are 1, 2 and 4, giving 1 + 4 + 16 = 21.
The special indices are 1, 2, 3 and 6, giving 4 + 49 + 1 + 9 = 63.

title: Find the K-th Character in String Game I
description:
Start with the string word = "a". Repeatedly build a new string: take the current word, change each letter to the next letter of the alphabet ('z' becomes 'a'), and append that new string to the end of word. Given an integer k, return the k-th character (1-indexed) of the word after enough steps that it has at least k characters.

Example: the word goes a -> ab -> abbc -> abbcbccd. The 5th character of abbcbccd is 'b', so for k = 5 the answer is 'b'.
hints: Keep appending transformed copies until the string is at least k characters long, then read the character at position k - 1.

test_cases.explanation: After two steps the word is "abbc" and the next step appends "bccd"; position 5 is 'b'.
Position 10 of the grown string is 'c'.

title: Check If Digits Are Equal in String After Operations I
description:
You are given a string `s` of digits, at least 3 characters long. Repeat this operation until only two digits are left: replace each pair of adjacent digits with the sum of the two digits modulo 10. For example, "1234" becomes "357" because 1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 4 = 7. Return true if the final two digits are equal, and false otherwise.

Example: "3902" becomes "292", and then "11". The two final digits are equal, so the answer is true.
hints: Apply the operation step by step until two digits remain. The string is short, so simulating is fast.

test_cases.explanation: 3902 -> 292 -> 11: the final two digits are both 1, so the result is true.
34789 -> 7157 -> 862 -> 48: the last two digits differ, so the answer is false.

title: Longest Subsequence With Limited Sum
description:
You are given an integer array `nums` of length n and an integer array `queries` of length m. For each query q, find the maximum number of elements you can pick from `nums` (you may choose any elements) whose sum is at most q. Return an array with one answer per query, in order.

Example: nums = [4, 5, 2, 1] and queries = [3, 10, 21]. For q = 3 you can pick 1 and 2 (sum 3): 2 elements. For q = 10 you can pick 1, 2 and 4 (sum 7), but adding 5 gives 12, so the answer is 3. For q = 21 all four fit (sum 12), so the answer is 4.
hints: Sort the numbers and build prefix sums. For each query, the answer is how many prefix sums are at most the query.

test_cases.explanation: The three answers are 2, 3 and 4.
The smallest number, 2, already exceeds 1, so the answer is 0.

title: Longest Palindrome by Concatenating Two Letter Words
description:
You are given an array `words` of two-letter strings (each word has exactly 2 lowercase letters; a word may appear more than once). You may pick words and place them in any order, using each word at most once, and concatenate them. Return the length of the longest possible palindrome you can form this way.

Example: words = ["lc", "cl", "gg"]. Put "lc" and "cl" on the outside ("lccl" is a palindrome) and "gg" in the middle ("lcggcl"). That has length 6, the longest possible.
constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Pair each word with its reverse when possible (each such pair contributes 4 characters). A word that reads the same both ways can pair with itself, and one leftover of those can go in the middle (adds 2 characters).

test_cases.explanation: The pairs lc/cl give 4 and gg goes in the middle for 2 more: 6 total.
The pairs ty/yt and lc/cl give 8 characters.

title: Jump Game VII
description:
You are given a binary string `s` (characters '0' and '1') and two integers minJump and maxJump. You start at index 0, which is always '0'. From index i you may jump to index j if s[j] == '0' and i + minJump <= j <= i + maxJump. Return true if you can reach the last index, and false otherwise.

Example: s = "011010", minJump = 2, maxJump = 3. Jump from 0 to 3 (s[3] = '0'), then from 3 to 5 (s[5] = '0'). The last index is reached, so the answer is true.
hints: Compute, for each index, whether it is reachable. An index is reachable if some reachable index lies in the window [j - maxJump, j - minJump]. A sliding count of reachable indices keeps this fast.

test_cases.explanation: The path 0 -> 3 -> 5 uses only '0' positions and reaches the end.
Jump from index 0 to index 1; both positions hold '0'.
From index 3 the only jumps land on 5 and 6, which are both '1', so the last index 7 cannot be reached.

title: Maximum Number of Jumps to Reach the Last Index
description:
You are given a 0-indexed array `nums` of n integers and an integer `target`. You start at index 0 and want to reach index n - 1. You may jump from index i to a later index j (i < j) only if the difference nums[j] - nums[i] lies in the range [-target, target]. Return the maximum number of jumps needed to reach the last index. If it is not possible, return -1.

Example: nums = [1, 3, 6, 4, 1, 2] and target = 2. One longest path is 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 5 with 3 jumps. The answer is 3.
hints: Let dp[j] be the longest jump count to reach j. Try every earlier reachable index i that satisfies the difference rule and take the best dp[i] + 1.

test_cases.explanation: The path 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 5 uses 3 jumps.
A path that uses all 5 jumps is possible with target 3.
All values differ, so no jump is allowed; the answer is -1.

title: Remove All Occurrences of a Substring
description:
Given strings `s` and `part`, repeatedly find the leftmost occurrence of `part` in `s` and remove it. Keep doing this while `part` still appears in `s`. Return the final string.

Example: s = "daabcbaabcbc", part = "abc". Remove the first "abc" to get "dabaabcbc". Remove the next leftmost "abc" to get "dababc". Remove the last one to get "dab".
constraints: s and part consist of lowercase English letters.
hints: Use a loop: find the leftmost occurrence, cut it out, and repeat. Python's str.replace with a count of 1 removes the leftmost match.

test_cases.explanation: Three removals leave "dab".
Four removals of xy: axxxxyyyyb -> axxxyyyb -> axxyyb -> axyb -> ab.

title: Longest Binary Subsequence Less Than or Equal to K
description:
You are given a binary string `s` and a positive integer k. Choose a subsequence of s (characters in their original order, not necessarily adjacent) that, read as a binary number, is at most k. Leading zeros are allowed in the subsequence. Return the length of the longest such subsequence.

Example: s = "1001010" and k = 5. The subsequence "00101" has value 5 and length 5. No longer subsequence stays within 5, so the answer is 5.
hints: Every 0 can always be taken without increasing the value. For the 1s, take the ones from the right while the value stays within k.

test_cases.explanation: The subsequence 00101 has length 5 and value 5.
